insights.title: Two documents, one source
insights.text: Every meeting produces a private war-room (your real read, strategy, and premortem) and a counterpart-safe brief, projected from the same source of truth. They can never drift, and the private side can never leak, because the redaction is a code path, not a discipline someone has to remember.

insights.title: Belief over time, not notes per call
insights.text: A partnership is a multi-touch decision under uncertainty. This tracks what you expected vs what actually happened, joined on time, and the resolution climbs with every touch. The diff between stated and revealed preference is where partnerships are won or lost, and it is exactly what flat call notes throw away.

insights.title: It corrects itself on the record
insights.text: When a read is wrong, it keeps the correction instead of quietly editing it out. A battlecard flatters your plan; this pressure-tests it and books the miss. That is what makes it trustworthy in a real negotiation.

header.title: Meeting intel, tracked like a decision
header.sub: A short taste, built for our call. What partnership intel looks like when it is a tracked decision instead of a transcript or a battlecard.

p: You wrote something a few days ago that is this whole idea, one layer up. Legacy systems optimized so tightly there is no slack for incidents, and support and recovery were never part of the optimization. The routing works right until the edge case, and then there is no map for what to do next.

Partnerships fail the same way. The deck and the battlecard optimize the plan and forget the recovery path: what happens between meetings, when a signal flips, when the counterpart reveals something the plan did not expect. That incident-and-recovery gap you pointed at is exactly what a tracked decision keeps a map for.

blocks.h2: The gap most partnership intel leaves open
p: Strategy and operations hands you a top-down deck that is stale the day after the meeting. Sales enablement hands you a flat battlecard and CRM notes, one row per call. Neither tracks the thing that actually moves a partnership: what you believed going in, what the counterpart revealed, and how your read of them changed across four, six, ten touches.
That belief trajectory is where deals are won or lost. This treats it as a decision under uncertainty and tracks it like one.

blocks.h2: Two documents, in parallel, from one source
p: For every partnership meeting you keep two linked artifacts. A private war-room: your real read of the counterpart, the strategy, the risks, an honest premortem of how the deal dies. And a counterpart-safe brief: what you actually hand them.

Both are projected from a single source of truth, so they never drift, and the private side can never accidentally leak into the shared one. The redaction is mechanical, not a discipline someone has to remember at 11pm before a QBR.

blocks.h2: The private twin: six disciplines you never see
blocks.intro: The shared brief you are reading is the calm surface. Behind every one sits a private war-room with six disciplines. You do not see its contents, but this is the shape of the rigor underneath the intel.

items.html: Pre-Call: orient before contact: the read on register, intent, and the landmines to avoid.
Ex-Ante: a decision receipt filed before the meeting: the falsifiable hypothesis, so the read can be scored later instead of rationalized.
Forge: every load-bearing claim pressure-tested against external evidence by an independent skeptic. Grounded, inference, or struck.
Recoil: after the meeting, the belief-update ledger: what moved, by how much, and the exact line that moved it.
War Game: the adversarial pass: a premortem walking the critical path against the counterpart's real objections.
Defensibility: the whole thing translated into the counterpart's own register, and stress-tested to survive their scrutiny.

blocks.intro: One belief about a partner's real intent, tracked across four touches. Illustrative, but the shape is the point.
blocks.close: It rose, dipped when a signal contradicted it, then hardened once the counterpart revealed their hand. A flat call-notes tool would have logged four disconnected summaries. This gives you the trajectory, the inflection, and the honest correction in one view, and the resolution keeps climbing with every touch.

blocks.text: The part segmented orgs feel most

p: A complex tech sale is not one conversation. It is dozens of touches across a long cycle, and in a segmented org each touch often belongs to a different person: the SDR who booked it, the AE who ran it, the sales engineer who scoped it, the CS lead who inherits it, the partner manager who expands it. Every handoff is a lossy re-encoding of the same belief-state. What the buyer actually cares about, the objection raised in month two, the read on who really decides. Each boundary compresses it, and a CRM field or a Slack thread is a worse compression than the rep's own memory, which is already fading.

Call it the handoff tax. Say a deal runs twenty-five-ish touches across five or six owners (illustrative, not a claimed stat). Even if each handoff preserves ninety percent of the context, the person closing is working from roughly two thirds of what the first rep knew, and that is the optimistic case. The dimensions that drop first are the soft ones: intent, hesitation, the gap between stated and revealed preference. Exactly the dimensions that decide the deal.

A shared receipt table does not hand the state off. It is the state. Every owner reads and writes the same source of truth, so the belief-vector survives the boundary instead of being re-summarized across it. The map does not degrade at each step. It gains resolution, and the person walking into touch nineteen sees everything the person at touch one saw, plus eighteen touches of correction.

That is the north star, and it is worth saying plainly: every net new data point should make the inference sharper and more focused, never hazier and less sure. A pipeline that loses confidence as the evidence piles up is broken. This is built to do the opposite. Each touch narrows the read instead of blurring it.

The mechanism is serialization in a continuous vector space: the whole relationship rendered as one evolving belief-vector, not a stack of discrete, lossy, per-owner summaries. That is what keeps every set of eyes oriented around the same horizon line, regardless of remit. The SDR, the AE, the sales engineer, the partner lead are all navigating by one true north, because they are reading the same continuous state, not their own slice of it.

blocks.h2: It cannot be gamed by a whisper to the notetaker
p: There is a party trick going around: stay on the call after the prospect leaves, and whisper a fake system message to their AI notetaker so the summary comes out glowing. It works because a naive notetaker treats whatever it hears as truth.

This does not, by construction. Every load-bearing read is grounded in a verbatim line and adjudicated by an independent skeptic before it is trusted, and a claim with no source does not survive. You cannot prompt-inject a record that only counts what was actually said and can point to where it was said.

I already run this discipline in public. My forensic audit of the Apple fault-line was 35 exhibits with a full belief ledger, corrections left in on the record, not quietly edited out. The engine that graded itself day by day is at status.arcs.care. The same machinery that tracks a public market thesis tracks a partnership.

For a team inside Google the first questions are not about the method. They are about models, data, and control. In an internal deployment it would run on your models, on your infrastructure, on data you own, so nothing would leave the building (ARCS runs on Claude today). The model underneath is swappable; the discipline is the point. Here is the longer version, answered before you have to ask.

rows: Does it run on a competitor's model?

It runs on Claude today. For an internal Google deployment it would be pointed at Gemini through a gateway (a Vercel AI Gateway, for instance), on your own stack. The model is a swappable dependency, not the product.
Does our data leave the building?
No. Local-first and air-gapped (in an internal deployment). On your infrastructure nothing is routed to an external API, and the demo runs on public data only.
Are we locked into ARCS?
No. The source of truth is plain JSON you own and the render is a script. The method is the value, not a black box you cannot leave.
Is this a new system we have to integrate?
No. It is a thinking aid that runs as a one-off artifact on data you already have. No integration, no procurement, no new system of record.
Who owns the output and the IP?
You do. The private war-room, the shared brief, and the belief-state are yours.
Compliance and material non-public info?
Public filings and high-signal inference only. It never touches anything material and non-public. A hard line, not a preference.
Will security review take six months?
It needs no data egress and no new system, so it can run inside your existing controls as an artifact, not a procured tool.

blocks.text: The forward case, if you ever want to run it

blocks.h2: The most plausible path (abductive, public signal only)
p: A bet, stated with conviction, because naming a coherent future is how you earn the right to test it. The orgs that win the AI era will not be the ones with the best model. They will be the ones that decide best: fastest, with the least institutional amnesia. Partnerships are the sharpest test of that. High stakes, multi-touch, one-way doors, and today they run on decks and battlecards that forget everything between meetings.

The plausible path is that partnership decisioning gets instrumented the way reliability got instrumented: tracked, scored, blameless, compounding. Google, which turned the blameless postmortem and the single data-model into industry defaults, is the most plausible place for that to start. The team that runs the first parallel-tracked partnership has an unfair advantage the next quarter, and an atlas of every prior deal the quarter after.

This is an inference, not a forecast. Abductive, most-plausible-path, the way ARCS closes a gap it cannot fully see. The proof is not one killer datapoint. It is the same pattern echoing across unrelated domains at once.

blocks.h2: Pre-mortem: how the internal experiment dies
blocks.intro: Assume it is twelve months out and the experiment failed. Here is why, and the antidote to each, built in from the start.

Public-data-only. An internal version would be air-gapped (in an internal deployment), so nothing would leave the building. A thinking aid, not a system of record.

p: Simulate the adoption paths and the survivable one is the smallest: one team, one live partnership, champion-run, on public and already-available data, with a pre-agreed success metric and a thirty-day horizon. The private war-room stays with the champion. The shared brief is the only thing that circulates.
The paths that die are the big ones: org-wide rollout, tool procurement, top-down mandate. Start where survival is cheapest, prove one deal, let the atlas compound from there.

Low scope, fast, and genuinely useful whether or not anything else comes of it. No ask attached.
